newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium stocks erode, price unimpressed.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium stocks erode, price unimpressed.

text.p: LME aluminium stocks kept falling relentlessly this week but futures prices shrugged it off, partially due to scepticism over how much of the material was going to consumers, analysts said.
In other metals, copper inventory declines began to fizzle-out and the zinc market breathed a sign of relief that expected deliveries of Chinese material failed to appear in Singapore.
Aluminium inventories in official London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses fell this week by 16,050 tonnes to 724,350 tonnes after dropping by a similar amount last week.
Since the beginning of the year, stocks have declined by 226,925 tonnes, or 23.9 percent.
Some in the market, however, are wary of the declines, and this scepticism is reflected in weak futures prices which have been in a medium term downtrend since mid-May.
"There are rather strong concerns that the material moving off the LME is not going to end-user demand," said analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton.
The market saw strong demand in the first part of the year as consumers restocked, but end users are now content to operate on a hand-to-mouth basis, he added.
Some of the metal coming out of LME warehouses appears to be going into consignment stocks.
More bullish analysts say that even though some of the stocks are not going to end-users they are still tied-up in financing operations and not available to the market.
Copper stocks took a bumpy ride, with a combination of small increases and declines, ending in a net fall of 600 tonnes.
Total stocks now stand at 132,625 tonnes, up 7,275 tonnes since the start of the year.

"Although it is too early to conclude that the stocks drawdown has ended, this tended to undermine sentiment," broker Brandeis said in a commentary on Thursday, the second consecutive day that stocks rose.
Stocks have been falling since mid-May, but the curve is flattening out and some players believe the summer lull is already beginning to be felt.
"The net increase in the stocks have started to suggest that copper may be swinging back into surplus," analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff said in a commentary.
Zinc stocks recorded a net decline for the week, but a string of daily falls was interrupted by an increase of 1,025 tonnes on Wednesday.
The metal was delivered into Italy, however, not Singapore, on which traders have been keeping a close eye after talk that more shipments from China would show up at that warehouse.
Fresh 4-1/2 year highs attained by three months prices this week of $1,375 were partially attributed to relief that the Chinese stocks failed to materialise.
"The concerns over Chinese deliveries have eased slightly and been put on a back burner, at least until the market sees a Singapore stock rise," Squires said.
Total stocks were at 422,325 tonnes, down 242,375 tonnes or 36.5 percent.
Nickel stocks rose by 1,416 tonnes to 52,380 tonnes this week, with the market's outlook pegged on how long workers at Inco's Sudbury operation would stay on strike.
If the stoppage ends up being lengthy, the Canadian firm may have to dip into LME stocks to make up lost production, analysts said.
